blocks.body:
This page is about one rule that joins multiplying and adding. If you do not know $7 \times 6$, you can split the 7 into $5 + 2$: five sixes are 30, two sixes are 12, and together they make 42. The rule that makes this work is called the distributive property (in England, the distributive law).

You will use it to find times facts from facts you know, to explain the area of a rectangle, to multiply bigger numbers in your head, and later to work with letters. You should already know what multiplication means ([[multiplication]]) and that numbers can be multiplied in any order ([[properties-of-operations]]).

blocks.title: Splitting a times fact
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to find a times fact you do not know by splitting it into two facts you do know.

Try this. Make 7 rows of 6 counters. Lay a pencil across the counters just under the fifth row. How many counters are above the pencil? How many are below it? How many are there altogether?

blocks.caption: 7 rows of 6 counters, split by a line under the fifth row. Above the line: 5 rows of 6 (filled), $5 \times 6 = 30$. Below it: 2 rows of 6 (open), $2 \times 6 = 12$. Altogether $30 + 12 = 42$, so $7 \times 6 = 42$.
blocks.alt: An array of 42 dots in 7 rows of 6. The top 5 rows are solid black dots; the bottom 2 rows are open blue circles, separated from the top by a dashed line. Labels: 5 rows of 6, 5 times 6 = 30; 2 rows of 6, 2 times 6 = 12.

blocks.title: Brackets
blocks.body:
Brackets ( ) show a part of a calculation to do first. (In the United States they are called parentheses.) $3 \times (4 + 2)$ means: first add, $4 + 2 = 6$, then multiply, $3 \times 6 = 18$.

Without brackets, multiplying is done before adding: $3 \times 4 + 2$ means $12 + 2 = 14$. The full set of rules for which part comes first is the order of operations, which has its own page.

blocks.title: Splitting a factor
blocks.body:
The two numbers that are multiplied are called factors. In $7 \times 6$ the factors are 7 and 6.

Seven rows of 6 are five rows of 6 and two more rows of 6. So we can split the factor 7 into $5 + 2$, multiply each part by 6, and add the two answers:
$$7 \times 6 = 5 \times 6 + 2 \times 6$$
Examples:

- $8 \times 7 = 8 \times 5 + 8 \times 2$ (the 7 is split into $5 + 2$).
- $6 \times 4 = 5 \times 4 + 1 \times 4$ (the 6 is split into $5 + 1$).

Non-example: $8 \times 7$ is not $8 \times 5 + 2$. Both parts of the 7 must be multiplied by 8, so the second part is $8 \times 2$, not 2.

blocks.title: The distributive property
blocks.body:
For any whole numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ (letters stand for numbers; the same rule also holds for fractions, decimals and negative numbers, as the last two sections explain):
$$a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c$$
The split factor can also come first:
$$(b + c) \times a = b \times a + c \times a$$
In words: multiplying a sum gives the same answer as multiplying each part and then adding.

Make an array for $a \times (b + c)$: $a$ rows, with $b + c$ counters in each row. Draw a line down the array after the first $b$ counters of every row.

Left of the line there are $a$ rows of $b$, which is $a \times b$ counters. Right of the line there are $a$ rows of $c$, which is $a \times c$ counters. Every counter is on exactly one side of the line, so the two parts together are all the counters: $a \times b + a \times c = a \times (b + c)$. Counters come in whole numbers, so this picture shows the rule for whole numbers.

For the second form, draw the line across the array between rows instead, as in the picture of $7 \times 6$ above.

blocks.title: Ways to see 7 times 6 as 5 times 6 plus 2 times 6
blocks.body: Each source shows the same split in its own way.

items.label: Equal groups
items.body: 7 groups of 6 are 5 groups of 6 and 2 more groups of 6. NCETM describes this split as partitioning the number of groups.

items.label: Array
items.body: 7 rows of 6, with a line under the fifth row: 5 rows above and 2 rows below. In Illustrative Mathematics, children match expressions such as $(5 \times 3) + (2 \times 3)$ to rectangles and shade the parts that the numbers stand for.

items.label: Building on fives
items.body: The Common Core progressions extend the $5 \times n$ pattern: 6, 7, 8 and 9 times a number are $5 \times n$ plus 1, 2, 3 or 4 more times the number. So $7 \times 6$ is $5 \times 6 = 30$ and 2 more sixes, $30 + 12 = 42$.

items.label: Symbols
items.body: $(5 + 2) \times 6 = 5 \times 6 + 2 \times 6$, which is the rule $(b + c) \times a = b \times a + c \times a$ with $b = 5$, $c = 2$ and $a = 6$.

blocks.title: Brackets change the answer
blocks.body: $8 \times (5 + 2)$ and $8 \times 5 + 2$ are different. The first is $8 \times 7 = 56$. The second multiplies first: $40 + 2 = 42$. England's curriculum makes the same point with $2 + 1 \times 3 = 5$ but $(2 + 1) \times 3 = 9$. When you split a factor, write the brackets or write both products in full.

blocks.title: For adults: the name can wait
blocks.body: The Common Core standard asks children to use the distributive property as a strategy and says in a footnote that they need not know its formal name. Illustrative Mathematics does not name it to Grade 3 pupils either; they talk about breaking a factor apart into smaller parts. Let the child use the split and explain it with a picture first; the word can come later.

blocks.title: For adults: when a child counts one by one
blocks.body: In the Illustrative Mathematics lesson, the teacher notes say that if a child counts single squares in a rectangle, the teacher asks how a product the child already knows could be used. At home you can do the same: do not tell the split, ask which product they already know that could help, such as $5 \times 6$ for $7 \times 6$.
You know that $8 \times 5 = 40$ and $8 \times 2 = 16$. Find $8 \times 7$.
blocks.solution:
Split the 7 into $5 + 2$, because you know the facts for 5 and 2.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 \times 7 &= 8 \times (5 + 2) \\ &= 8 \times 5 + 8 \times 2 \\ &= 40 + 16 \\ &= 56 \end{aligned}$$

blocks.body: You know that $6 \times 5 = 30$. Use it to find $7 \times 5$.
blocks.solution:
7 fives are 6 fives and one more five. Split the 7 into $6 + 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7 \times 5 &= (6 + 1) \times 5 \\ &= 6 \times 5 + 1 \times 5 \\ &= 30 + 5 = 35 \end{aligned}$$

items.a: No. The 2 must be multiplied by 6 too: $6 \times 5 + 6 \times 2 = 30 + 12 = 42$, but $6 \times 5 + 2 = 32$.

items.hint: 6 sevens are 5 sevens and one more seven.
What must be added to 5 to make 8?

items.q: Sam says $4 \times 9 = 4 \times 5 + 4 = 24$. What went wrong? What is the right answer?
items.hint: The 9 was split into $5 + 4$. Was the 4 multiplied?
items.solution: Sam forgot to multiply the 4 by 4. $4 \times 9 = 4 \times 5 + 4 \times 4 = 20 + 16 = 36$.

blocks.body:
- A factor is one of the numbers being multiplied.
- You can split a factor into two parts, multiply each part, and add: $7 \times 6 = 5 \times 6 + 2 \times 6$.
- The rule is $a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c$, the distributive property (distributive law).
- An array split by a line shows why: every counter is in exactly one part.
- Both parts must be multiplied, and brackets show what is done first.

blocks.title: Rectangles split in two
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to show the distributive property with the area of a rectangle, use a cut rectangle to find a product, and find the area of an L-shaped figure made of rectangles.

Try this. On squared paper, draw a rectangle 4 squares tall and 8 squares long. Colour the first 3 columns. How many squares are coloured? How many are not? How many squares are in the whole rectangle?

blocks.title: Area
blocks.body: The area of a shape is the number of unit squares that cover it, with no gaps and no overlaps. A rectangle with sides $a$ and $b$ (whole numbers) is covered by $a$ rows of $b$ squares, so its area is $a \times b$. Area has its own page: [[area-volume]].

blocks.caption: A rectangle 4 squares tall and $3 + 5 = 8$ squares long, tiled with 32 unit squares and cut into two parts: a 4 by 3 part (hatched, 12 squares) and a 4 by 5 part (20 squares). $4 \times 8 = 4 \times 3 + 4 \times 5 = 12 + 20 = 32$.
blocks.alt: A grid of 4 rows and 8 columns of squares. The first 3 columns are hatched blue and labelled 4 times 3 = 12; the other 5 columns are white and labelled 4 times 5 = 20. A thick line separates the two parts. The side is labelled 4; the top is labelled 3 and 5.

blocks.title: A rectangle cut in two
blocks.body:
A rectangle with whole-number sides $a$ and $b + c$ can be cut into a rectangle $a$ by $b$ and a rectangle $a$ by $c$. Its area is the total of the two areas:
$$a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c$$
The Common Core asks Grade 3 pupils to show this with tiles for one rectangle and then to use such area models to explain the distributive property.

Cutting does not add or remove any squares. Every square of the big rectangle lies in exactly one of the two parts. So the squares of the big rectangle, $a \times (b + c)$ of them, are the squares of the first part, $a \times b$, together with the squares of the second part, $a \times c$. Area is additive: when a shape is cut into pieces that do not overlap, its area is the sum of the areas of the pieces.

blocks.title: One rectangle, several cuts
blocks.body: Illustrative Mathematics shows one 3 by 6 rectangle cut in two different ways. Cutting the 6 into $5 + 1$ gives $3 \times 5 + 3 \times 1 = 15 + 3 = 18$. Cutting the rectangle into two equal halves gives $2 \times (3 \times 3) = 2 \times 9 = 18$; that second way uses grouping ([[properties-of-operations]]) rather than the distributive property. Both give the same area, 18.

blocks.title: For adults: match every number to the picture
blocks.body: Illustrative Mathematics has children match expressions to rectangles and shade the parts. For $(5 \times 3) + (2 \times 3)$ and a rectangle with 3 rows of 7: the 7 has been made from 5 and 2, and the 3 appears in both products because both parts are 3 rows tall. It helps to ask the child to point to each number in the picture before working out the answer.
Use an area model to find $4 \times 7$.
blocks.solution:
Draw a rectangle 4 tall and 7 long. Cut the 7 into $5 + 2$, because fives are easy.

The left part is 4 by 5, area $4 \times 5 = 20$. The right part is 4 by 2, area $4 \times 2 = 8$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 \times 7 &= 4 \times (5 + 2) \\ &= 20 + 8 = 28 \end{aligned}$$

blocks.body: A rectangle has 8 rows of 8 squares. Tyler writes $(5 \times 8) + (3 \times 8)$ for it. How did Tyler cut the rectangle, and what is its area?
blocks.solution:
$5 + 3 = 8$, so Tyler cut the 8 rows into 5 rows and 3 rows. Each row has 8 squares.

Top part: $5 \times 8 = 40$. Bottom part: $3 \times 8 = 24$.

Area: $40 + 24 = 64$, which is $8 \times 8$.

blocks.caption: An L-shaped figure tiled with 18 unit squares and cut by a dashed line into two rectangles: a 2 by 3 part on top (hatched, 6 squares) and a 6 by 2 part below (12 squares). $6 + 12 = 18$.
blocks.alt: An L-shaped figure made of unit squares: a bottom block 6 squares wide and 2 tall, and above its left end a hatched blue block 2 squares wide and 3 tall. A dashed line separates the two blocks. Labels: 2 times 3 = 6 for the top block, 6 times 2 = 12 for the bottom block, whole shape 6 + 12 = 18.

blocks.body: Find the area of the L-shaped figure above, which is tiled with unit squares. It is not a rectangle, so the rule $a \times b$ cannot be used on all of it at once.
blocks.solution:
Cut it into two rectangles that do not overlap, along the dashed line.

Top part: 3 rows of 2 squares, $3 \times 2 = 6$.

Bottom part: 2 rows of 6 squares, $2 \times 6 = 12$.

Area is additive, so the whole area is $6 + 12 = 18$ square units.

The same shape can be cut another way: a tall part 2 wide and 5 tall on the left, $2 \times 5 = 10$, and a part 4 wide and 2 tall on the right, $4 \times 2 = 8$. Again $10 + 8 = 18$.

items.q: A 3 by 7 rectangle is cut into a 3 by 5 part and a 3 by 2 part. What are the three areas?
Which product does a rectangle with sides 6 and $4 + 3$ show?
Can the parts of a cut rectangle overlap?
items.a: No. Every square must be in exactly one part, or some squares would be counted twice.

items.q: An L-shaped figure is cut into a 4 by 3 rectangle and a 2 by 5 rectangle. What is its area?
A rectangle 6 by 9 is cut into a 6 by 5 part and a 6 by 4 part. Find the area of each part and of the whole.
items.hint: Multiply the sides of each part.
items.solution: $6 \times 5 = 30$ and $6 \times 4 = 24$. The whole is $30 + 24 = 54$, which is $6 \times 9$.

items.q: A rectangle has sides 5 and $3 + 6$. Find its area in two ways.
items.hint: Either add first, or find the two parts first.
items.solution: Adding first: $5 \times 9 = 45$. In parts: $5 \times 3 + 5 \times 6 = 15 + 30 = 45$. Both give 45.

items.q: Write an expression with two products for a 4 by 9 rectangle cut after 5 columns. Then find the area.
items.hint: The 9 columns become 5 columns and 4 columns.

items.q: Noah writes $(5 \times 3) + (2 \times 3)$. Draw or describe his rectangle and find its area.
items.hint: Which number is in both products?
items.solution: 3 is in both products, so every part is 3 rows tall; the other side is $5 + 2 = 7$. It is a 3 by 7 rectangle cut into 3 by 5 and 3 by 2. Area $15 + 6 = 21$.

items.q: Find $7 \times 8$ with an area model. Choose your own cut.
items.solution: One way: $7 \times 5 + 7 \times 3 = 35 + 21 = 56$. Any cut gives 56, for example $7 \times 4 + 7 \times 4 = 28 + 28 = 56$.

items.q: A floor is made of a 5 by 4 rectangle and a 3 by 2 rectangle joined side by side so that they do not overlap. What is the area of the floor?
items.hint: Find the area of each rectangle first, then add.
items.solution: $5 \times 4 = 20$ and $3 \times 2 = 6$, so the area is $20 + 6 = 26$ square units.

blocks.body:
- The area of an $a$ by $b$ rectangle is $a \times b$ squares.
- Cut a rectangle with sides $a$ and $b + c$ into two rectangles: $a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c$.
- No square is lost or counted twice, so the areas add up.
- Every number in the expression can be found in the picture.
- A shape cut into rectangles that do not overlap has an area equal to the sum of their areas, even when the whole shape is not a rectangle.

blocks.title: Multiplying bigger numbers
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number by splitting it into tens and ones.

Try this. How could $30 \times 7$ and $9 \times 7$ help you find $39 \times 7$?

blocks.title: Splitting into tens and ones
blocks.body:
Place value ([[place-value]]) tells us that $39 = 30 + 9$: 3 tens and 9 ones. Multiplying tens is easy: $30 \times 7$ is 3 tens times 7, which is 21 tens, or 210 ([[multiplication]]). So split the bigger number into its tens and its ones, multiply each part, and add:
$$\begin{aligned} 39 \times 7 &= 30 \times 7 + 9 \times 7 \\ &= 210 + 63 = 273 \end{aligned}$$
England's curriculum asks Year 4 pupils to use the distributive law in exactly this way to multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number. The Common Core asks Grade 4 pupils to explain such products with equations, arrays or area models.

blocks.caption: An area model (not drawn to scale, no squares shown) for $39 \times 7$. The long side 39 is cut into 30 and 9. The parts have areas $30 \times 7 = 210$ and $9 \times 7 = 63$ (hatched), so $39 \times 7 = 273$.
blocks.alt: A long rectangle with height labelled 7 and length split into 30 and 9. The large left part reads 30 times 7 = 210; the narrow hatched orange right part reads 9 times 7 = 63. Below: 39 times 7 = 210 + 63 = 273.

blocks.title: Ways to split a bigger number
blocks.body: The sources split the bigger number in different ways; each split uses the same rule.

items.label: Area model
items.body: A rectangle without squares, one side cut into two parts; the two areas are added. In Illustrative Mathematics Grade 3 Unit 4 Lesson 16, children compare ways to cut 23 for $4 \times 23$ ($12 + 11$, $15 + 8$, $10 + 13$, $20 + 3$) and find that tens and ones is the most practical cut. Common Core 4.NBT.B.5 asks for area models like this with larger numbers.

items.label: Money
items.body: OpenStax opens with three friends who each pay 9 dollars and 1 quarter and counts the dollars and the quarters separately. Here is the same idea with cents: each pays 9 dollars and 25 cents, so $3 \times 9 = 27$ dollars and $3 \times 25 = 75$ cents, which is 27 dollars and 75 cents.

items.label: Take away
items.body: Split $39$ as $40 - 1$ instead: $40 \times 7 - 1 \times 7 = 280 - 7 = 273$. This uses the take-away form of the rule, in the next section.

blocks.title: Multiply both parts
blocks.body: A common slip is to multiply only the first part: $39 \times 7 = 30 \times 7 + 9 = 219$ is wrong. Paul Dawkins's list of algebra errors says people often multiply the first part and forget the second; OpenStax says to multiply the outside number by every part. The 9 must be multiplied by 7: $210 + 63 = 273$.

blocks.title: Written methods
blocks.body: The written methods for multiplying, short multiplication and long multiplication, record the same splitting in columns: each digit's part is multiplied and the parts are added. The Common Core progressions say the distributive property is at the heart of Grades 3 to 5, including multi-digit multiplication. The written methods have their own page, Long multiplication.
Find $23 \times 4$.
Three friends each buy a ticket costing 9 dollars and 25 cents. How much do they pay altogether?
blocks.solution:
Split the price into dollars and cents.

Dollars: $3 \times 9 = 27$ dollars.

Cents: $3 \times 25 = 75$ cents.

Altogether: 27 dollars and 75 cents.

blocks.body: Find $12 \times 14$.

items.q: Split 46 into tens and ones and find $46 \times 3$.
Find $125 \times 4$ by splitting 125 into three parts.

blocks.body:
- Split a two-digit number into tens and ones: $39 = 30 + 9$.
- Multiply each part and add: $39 \times 7 = 210 + 63 = 273$.
- An area model shows the two parts as two rectangles.
- Every part must be multiplied; the written methods use the same idea.

blocks.title: Splitting with take-away
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to find a product by starting from an easy product nearby and taking away the extra.

Try this. Make 7 rows of 10 counters, which is 70. Take away the last counter of every row. How many counters did you take away? How many rows are there, and how many counters are in each row now?

blocks.caption: 7 rows of 10 counters make $7 \times 10 = 70$. The last counter of each row is crossed out: $7 \times 1 = 7$ counters. What is left is 7 rows of 9, so $7 \times 9 = 70 - 7 = 63$.
blocks.alt: An array of 7 rows of 10 dots. In each row the first 9 dots are black and the tenth is a red circle with a red cross. Labels: 7 times 10 = 70 counters; take away 7 times 1 = 7; 7 times 9 = 70 - 7 = 63.

blocks.title: The take-away form
blocks.body:
For any numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ with $c$ not bigger than $b$:
$$a \times (b - c) = a \times b - a \times c$$
For example, $7 \times 9 = 7 \times (10 - 1) = 7 \times 10 - 7 \times 1$.

Make $a$ rows of $b$ counters: that is $a \times b$ counters. Take away the last $c$ counters of every row. You took away $a$ rows of $c$, which is $a \times c$ counters. What is left is $a$ rows of $b - c$, which is $a \times (b - c)$. So $a \times (b - c) = a \times b - a \times c$.

blocks.title: Ways to find 7 times 9
blocks.body: Four ways from four sources; all give 63.

items.label: Turn, then split
items.body: NCETM also turns the fact around first: $7 \times 9 = 9 \times 7 = 9 \times 5 + 9 \times 2 = 45 + 18 = 63$.

items.label: Nines from tens
items.body: The Common Core progressions build the nines from the tens: $2 \times 9 = 2 \times 10 - 2 \times 1 = 18$; in the same way $7 \times 9 = 70 - 7$.

items.label: Rectangle
items.body: A 7 by 9 rectangle cut into a 7 by 5 part and a 7 by 4 part: $35 + 28 = 63$.

blocks.title: Take away the right amount
blocks.body: $7 \times 9$ is not $70 - 1$. You take away one counter from each of the 7 rows, so you take away $7 \times 1 = 7$, not 1. This is the same slip as forgetting to multiply the second part.
Find $99 \times 6$.
Find $9 \times 8$ from the tens.
blocks.solution:
$9 = 10 - 1$, so 9 eights are 10 eights take away one eight.
$$\begin{aligned} 9 \times 8 &= 10 \times 8 - 1 \times 8 \\ &= 80 - 8 = 72 \end{aligned}$$

blocks.body:
- Start from an easy product and take away the extra: $7 \times 9 = 70 - 7$.
- The rule is $a \times (b - c) = a \times b - a \times c$.
- Take away $a \times c$, one part from every row, not just $c$.
- Numbers just below a ten or a hundred, like 9, 29, 99, are good for this.

blocks.title: Putting products together
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to spot two products that share a factor and join them into one easier product.

Try this. There are 3 boxes of 8 pens and 7 more boxes of 8 pens. How many boxes are there? How many pens?

blocks.caption: Each row is a box of 8 pens. 3 boxes (dotted, green) and 7 boxes (plain) make 10 boxes: $3 \times 8 + 7 \times 8 = 24 + 56 = 80 = 10 \times 8$.
blocks.alt: Ten rows of eight small squares. The top three rows are dotted green and labelled 3 times 8 = 24; below a dashed line, seven plain rows are labelled 7 times 8 = 56. Underneath: 10 times 8 = 80.

blocks.title: Reading the rule backwards
blocks.body:
An equals sign works in both directions ([[equality-equal-sign]]), so the distributive property can be read from right to left:
$$a \times b + a \times c = a \times (b + c)$$
$$a \times b - a \times c = a \times (b - c)$$
When two products share a factor, add (or subtract) the other factors first and multiply once. The shared factor is called a common factor.

Each product counts groups of the same size. $3 \times 8$ is 3 groups of 8 and $7 \times 8$ is 7 groups of 8. Together they are $3 + 7 = 10$ groups of 8, which is $10 \times 8$. Taking away groups works the same way. This is the distributive property with the two sides swapped.

blocks.title: Only a common factor can be pulled out
blocks.body: $3 \times 8 + 7 \times 6$ cannot be joined into one product of the form $(3 + 7) \times \square$: the groups have different sizes, 8 and 6. Work out each product: $24 + 42 = 66$. NCETM presents joining as a way to solve two-part problems whose two products have a common factor.
Find $3 \times 8 + 7 \times 8$.
blocks.solution:
Both products have the factor 8.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 \times 8 + 7 \times 8 &= (3 + 7) \times 8 \\ &= 10 \times 8 = 80 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $24 + 56 = 80$.

blocks.body: A shop had 12 packs of 6 eggs and sold 2 packs. How many eggs are left?
blocks.solution:
Eggs left: $12 \times 6 - 2 \times 6$. Both products have the factor 6.
$$\begin{aligned} 12 \times 6 - 2 \times 6 &= (12 - 2) \times 6 \\ &= 10 \times 6 = 60 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $72 - 12 = 60$.

items.q: What is the common factor in $4 \times 9 + 6 \times 9$?

items.a: Yes: the common factor is 5, and $3 + 7 = 10$. Both give 50.

items.q: Tickets cost 8 dollars. A cinema sells 13 tickets on Monday and 7 on Tuesday. How much money does it take?
Find $11 \times 7 - 1 \times 7$, and explain why $11 \times 7 - 1 \times 6$ cannot be done the same way.
items.hint: Look for a factor in both products.
items.solution: $(11 - 1) \times 7 = 70$. In $11 \times 7 - 1 \times 6$ there is no common factor, so work out each part: $77 - 6 = 71$.

blocks.body:
- Two products with a common factor can be joined: $3 \times 8 + 7 \times 8 = 10 \times 8$.
- This is the distributive property read from right to left.
- It works for taking away too: $12 \times 6 - 2 \times 6 = 10 \times 6$.
- It needs a factor that is the same in both products.

blocks.title: The rule with letters
blocks.body:
This section is for older readers (England Year 5 and 6, United States Grade 6 and later). After it you will be able to multiply out a bracket such as $3(x + 4)$, and put a common factor back outside a bracket.

Try this. Think of a number. Add 4, then multiply by 3. Now take your number again: multiply it by 3, then add 12. Do you get the same answer? Try another number.

blocks.title: Letters and how products are written
blocks.body:
In algebra a letter such as $x$ stands for a number. A number written next to a letter means multiply: $3x$ means $3 \times x$. A number next to a bracket also means multiply: $3(x + 4)$ means $3 \times (x + 4)$. OpenStax also uses a raised dot, $3 \cdot 4 = 12$.

With letters for all three numbers, England's Year 5 notes write the distributive law as $a(b + c) = ab + ac$.

blocks.title: The distributive property with letters
blocks.body:
For any numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ (whole numbers to begin with):
$$a(b + c) = ab + ac$$
$$a(b - c) = ab - ac$$
$$(b + c)a = ba + ca$$
Multiplying out the bracket is often called expanding the bracket. OpenStax says to use the rule when the terms inside the bracket cannot be added, as in $x + 4$.

blocks.caption: OpenStax draws arrows from the number outside the bracket to each term inside: the 3 multiplies the $x$ and the 3 multiplies the 4, so $3(x + 4) = 3x + 12$.
blocks.alt: The expression 3(x + 4) with two blue curved arrows starting at the 3, one ending at x and one ending at 4, followed by = 3 times x + 3 times 4 = 3x + 12.

blocks.body:
When the letters stand for whole numbers, the array picture above is a proof, whatever the numbers of rows and columns. The Common Core progressions note that distributivity holds in every number system met at school, so the rule is also used for fractions, decimals and negative numbers; the reasons come later (see Looking ahead).

You can also check a case, though one check is not a proof. OpenStax puts $y = 10$ into $6(5y + 1)$ and into $30y + 6$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6(5 \times 10 + 1) &= 6 \times 51 = 306 \\ 30 \times 10 + 6 &= 300 + 6 = 306 \end{aligned}$$
The Common Core calls two expressions equivalent when they name the same number whatever value the letter has.
Multiply out $3(x + 4)$.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the 3 by each term inside the bracket.
$$\begin{aligned} 3(x + 4) &= 3 \cdot x + 3 \cdot 4 \\ &= 3x + 12 \end{aligned}$$

blocks.body: Multiply out $2(x - 3)$ and $m(n - 4)$.
blocks.solution:
$$2(x - 3) = 2x - 2 \cdot 3 = 2x - 6$$
$$m(n - 4) = mn - 4m$$
OpenStax writes $4m$ rather than $m4$: by the commutative property the number can go first.

blocks.body: Write $24x + 18y$ with a common factor outside a bracket.
blocks.solution:
Both 24 and 18 are in the 6 times table: $24 = 6 \times 4$ and $18 = 6 \times 3$. So
$$24x + 18y = 6 \cdot 4x + 6 \cdot 3y$$
and reading the rule backwards,
$$24x + 18y = 6(4x + 3y)$$

blocks.body: Simplify $8 - 2(x + 3)$.
blocks.solution:
Multiply first: $2(x + 3) = 2x + 6$. The whole of $2x + 6$ is taken away from 8, so both parts are taken away.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 - 2(x + 3) &= 8 - 2x - 6 \\ &= 2 - 2x \end{aligned}$$
OpenStax writes the answer as $-2x + 2$, which is the same.

blocks.title: Multiply every term inside the bracket
blocks.body: $4(x + 2)$ is $4x + 8$, not $4x + 2$. Paul Dawkins lists this as one of the two main errors he meets regularly: people multiply the first term by the outside number and ignore the second term.

blocks.title: Take away the whole bracket
blocks.body: In $8 - 2(x + 3)$ both $2x$ and $6$ are taken away. Writing $8 - 2x + 6$ takes away only part of the bracket. Dawkins stresses that the whole expression must be subtracted.

blocks.title: Dividing by a sum does not split
blocks.body: Multiplication spreads over the parts of a sum, but dividing by a sum does not. $12 \div (2 + 4) = 12 \div 6 = 2$, while $12 \div 2 + 12 \div 4 = 6 + 3 = 9$. Dawkins gives the letter version: $\frac{1}{x + y}$ is not $\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}$.

blocks.title: For older readers: a negative factor
blocks.body:
The rule also holds when the outside number is negative. Every term inside is multiplied by it, so every sign changes. OpenStax:
$$-2(4y + 1) = -8y - 2$$
$$-(y + 5) = -y - 5$$
(a minus sign in front of a bracket means multiply by $-1$). Check the first with $y = 3$: $-2(12 + 1) = -26$ and $-24 - 2 = -26$.

blocks.title: Names and ways of writing
blocks.body: Books and countries name and write the rule differently.

rows.text: The distributive law (and distributivity); Year 4 pupils use it to multiply two-digit numbers by one-digit numbers; the Year 5 notes write $a(b + c) = ab + ac$. Calculations are grouped with brackets.
The distributive property, used in Grade 3 as a strategy; a footnote says pupils need not use the formal name. Brackets are called parentheses.
Grade 3 pupils say they break apart a factor or decompose a rectangle into smaller rectangles; the property is named only in the teacher notes.
Distributive Property, in three forms: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$, $a(b - c) = ab - ac$ and $(b + c)a = ba + ca$. Products are written $3x$, $a(b + c)$ or with a raised dot.

items.hint: Two terms inside, so two products.

items.q: Multiply out $9(3y + 8)$, then check both forms with $y = 2$.
Write $15a + 10b$ with a common factor outside a bracket.
items.hint: 15 and 10 are both in the 5 times table.
Multiply out first, then take away both parts.

items.q: Ali writes $2(x + 5) = 2x + 5$. Show with $x = 1$ that this is wrong, then correct it.
items.solution: Left: $2(1 + 5) = 12$. Right: $2 + 5 = 7$. They differ, so it is wrong. Correct: $2(x + 5) = 2x + 10$, and $2 + 10 = 12$.

blocks.body:
- With letters the rule is $a(b + c) = ab + ac$; $3x$ means $3 \times x$.
- Multiply the outside number by every term inside: $3(x + 4) = 3x + 12$.
- Read backwards, it puts a common factor outside: $24x + 18y = 6(4x + 3y)$.
- A minus sign before a bracket takes away every term inside.
- Dividing by a sum does not split into parts.

blocks.title: Looking ahead
blocks.body:
Splitting both numbers into tens and ones turns $12 \times 14$ into four small products. The Common Core asks Grade 4 pupils to multiply two two-digit numbers in ways like this, and England's curriculum asks for long multiplication, which records the same products, in Years 5 and 6. In algebra the same rule turns one expression into an equivalent one, as in $3(2 + x) = 6 + 3x$, and it multiplies out brackets that contain square roots: $\sqrt{2}(3 + \sqrt{2}) = 3\sqrt{2} + 2$.

The Common Core progressions note that distributivity holds in every number system met at school, up to the complex numbers. In higher algebra it becomes part of a definition: a ring ([[rings]]) is a set with an addition and a multiplication in which $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ and $(a + b)c = ac + bc$ always hold. The rule on this page is what ties the two operations of a ring together.
